“The silent stones must surely groan for fire and conflagration. They must surely long to be destroyed. They must surely beg to be delivered from the touching and gawking of the educated Wolff and his companions.”

Carl Schmitt read these lines with great approval when they appeared. At the same time, however, as part of his service with the deputy general command in Munich, he was himself required to order the confiscation of anti-war literature.
Of Theodor Haecker, whom he also met personally during this period, Schmitt said:
Schmitt later became more critical of Haecker. See below, pp. 131 f., entry for 2 July 1948.
good old Hall — Schmitt is referring to William Edward Hall, A Treatise on International Law, 8th ed., ed. A. Pearce Higgins, Oxford 1924. Schmitt’s copy survives in his papers, RW 265 No. 25814.
Strupp — Karl Strupp (1886–1940), scholar of international law.
Lauterpacht — Hersch Lauterpacht (1897–1960), scholar of international law.
something I noticed years ago while reading Westlake — John Westlake (1828–1913), British scholar of international law. Schmitt is probably referring to Nomos, pp. 203 and 210.
“impatience of justice” — See BW EJ, p. 232.
Ernest Nys — (1851–1920), Belgian scholar of international law.

Cardinal Mercier’s Christmas pastoral letter of 1914 — The Primate of Belgium was regarded, especially because of his pastoral letter Patriotisme et Endurance, as the intellectual leader of resistance to the occupation of his country.
See Désiré Mercier, Patriotisme et Endurance. Lettre pastorale de S. É. le Card. Mercier, Archevêque de Malines, The Hague 1914. German edition: Vaterlandsliebe und Ausdauer, Lausanne 1915.
Schmitt thought very highly of Cardinal Mercier. See RK, p. 11.
L’initié tue l’initiateur — “The initiate kills the initiator.”
The sentence comes from the French writer and philosopher of history Pierre-Simon Ballanche (1776–1846).
See Ballanche, Oeuvres de M. Ballanche, Vol. 4, Paris/Geneva 1830, p. 487.
See also the note below to p. 309 and BW Sombart.
W. Fraenger’s Grand Master of the free brotherhood — See Wilhelm Fraenger, Hieronymus Bosch. Das Tausendjährige Reich. Grundzüge e. Auslegung, Coburg 1947.
Schmitt assisted Fraenger with his Bosch research during the war.
See Wilhelm Fraenger, “Korrespondenz mit Hans Arp, Carl Schmitt und Franz Roh,” in Sinn und Form 57, 2005, pp. 303–330.
Mirko Jelusich — (1886–1969), National Socialist writer and author of popular historical novels.
the millennium of the new Ewe — In Stefan George’s private vocabulary, Ewe means “age” or “era.”
Hail to me that I see those who have been seized — From poem II, written at the outbreak of war in 1914, in Rainer Maria Rilke’s cycle Fünf Gesänge.
See R. M. Rilke, Werke. Kommentierte Ausgabe in vier Bänden, ed. Manfred Engel et al., Vol. 2, Frankfurt am Main 1996, p. 107.

the “Stahl” affair — The constitutional lawyer Friedrich Julius Stahl (1802–1861), originally named Jolson, was a Jewish convert to Christianity who explicitly grounded his conservative legal and political theory in Christianity.
On Freisler, see the note above to p. 74.
Barbey d’Aurevilly — Jules Amédée Barbey d’Aurevilly (1808–1889), French anti-modernist writer greatly admired by Schmitt.
Hadamovsky — Eugen Hadamovsky (1904–1945), specialist in National Socialist propaganda.

His book Propaganda und nationale Macht. Die Organisation der öffentlichen Meinung für die nationale Politik, Oldenburg 1933, was extensively used by Hannah Arendt for the section “Totalitarian Propaganda” in her book The Burden of Our Time, London 1951—later published in German as Elemente und Ursprünge totaler Herrschaft.
Schmitt’s copy survives in his papers, RW 265 No. 22551.
“The advantages of a propaganda that constantly ‘adds the power of organization’ to the feeble and unreliable voice of argument …”
Youth Without Goethe — Max Kommerell, Jugend ohne Goethe, Frankfurt am Main 1931.
In his own copy, Schmitt added the handwritten words “but with Hölderlin” to the title. The copy is privately owned.
Norbert von Hellingrath — (1888–1916), Germanist who discovered Hölderlin’s late hymns and published them in 1916.
meeting with Joachim Schoeps — Hans-Joachim Schoeps (1909–1980), conservative German-Jewish historian of religion.
In 1951 there was a brief exchange of letters between Schoeps and Schmitt.
See Frank-Lothar Kroll, Geschichtswissenschaft in politischer Absicht. Hans-Joachim Schoeps und Preußen, Berlin 2010, Appendix IV, pp. 92 f.
Cramer von Laue — Constantin Cramer von Laue (1906–1991), jurist. He studied under Schmitt during the 1930s and from 1951 onward worked for the Federal German government in a variety of roles.
Blüher’s debate about Israel — Hans Blüher/Hans-Joachim Schoeps, Streit um Israel. Ein jüdisch-christliches Gespräch, Hamburg 1933.
Gundolf — Friedrich Gundolf (1880–1931), Germanist and poet.
read Kafka — See Schmitt to Mohler, 26 December 1953, BW Mohler, p. 147:
The German has no time just now, He has to Kafka read; He strains himself and stands prepared For Kafka to cure him instead.
Gerhard Hess — (1907–1983), scholar of Romance languages. In 1938 he completed his habilitation at Berlin University with a study of Gassendi, discussed below, and then taught there as a lecturer.
In the early 1940s, while working for the Leibniz Commission of the Prussian Academy, Hess helped Schmitt verify quotations from Leibniz.
See F.-R. Hausmann in Romanistische Zeitschrift für Literaturgeschichte 23, 1999, p. 410.
After 1945 Hess became an influential figure in German academic administration, serving as president of the West German Rectors’ Conference and of the German Research Foundation.
edition of the Anti-Lucretius — Melchior de Polignac, Anti-Lucretius, sive de deo et natura, libri novem. Opus posthumum, Vols. 1–2, Paris 1754.
At Christmas 1968 Schmitt gave this edition to Rainer Specht with the dedication:
“with reference to Epirrhosis II, p. 699 ff.”

Shortly before this, R. Specht had published the essay “Über Polignacs ‘Antilucretius’” in the Schmitt Festschrift Epirrhosis, Berlin 1968, Vol. 2, pp. 697–707. The essay also discusses the physical phenomena mentioned here and Polignac’s relationship to Cartesianism.
Eripuit fulmen Jovi — “He wrested the thunderbolt from Jove.”

The idea ultimately goes back to Lucretius’s De rerum natura, which in turn refers to Epicurus. The phrase itself, however, probably first took this form in the Roman poet Marcus Manilius’s Astronomica, around 12 BC:
Eripuitque Jovi fulmen, viresque tonandi, Et sonitum ventis concessit, nubibus ignem.
“And he took from Jove the thunderbolt and the power to thunder, leaving sound to the winds and fire to the clouds.”
De Polignac quotes an altered version of the line in the first book of his Anti-Lucretius, where it refers to Epicurus:
Coeli tonitralia templa lacessens, Eripuit, fulmenque Jovi Phoeboque sagittas.
“Challenging the thundering temples of heaven, he took the thunderbolt from Jove and the arrows from Phoebus.”
During the eighteenth century the phrase became a familiar slogan of the Enlightenment, usually in altered form.

It appeared, for example, on the bust of Benjamin Franklin made by Houdon. Franklin, the inventor of the lightning rod, was celebrated there with a reference to In tyrannos—“against tyrants”—joining the conquest of lightning to a militant hostility toward traditional authority and religion.
Schmitt was suspicious of this celebration of humanism and Promethean reason.
See his letter to Ernst Jünger of 23 August 1955, BW EJ, pp. 284 and 723 f.
His skepticism reaches its clearest form at the end of Political Theology II, where eripuit fulmen Jovi is once again taken up critically.
See C. Schmitt, Politische Theologie II. Die Legende von der Erledigung jeder Politischen Theologie, Berlin 1970, p. 126.

your Gassendi — Gerhard Hess, Pierre Gassend. Der französische Späthumanismus und das Problem von Wissen und Glauben, Berliner Beiträge zur romanischen Philologie 9, 3/4, Jena/Leipzig 1939; also submitted as Hess’s habilitation thesis at Berlin University in 1938.
Schmitt owned a presentation copy inscribed to him by the author: RWN 260 No. 218.
Gassendo amatus surculus erroris — “The offshoot of error loved by Gassendi.”
This refers to lines 389 ff. of Polignac’s Anti-Lucretius:
… metuo, ne surculus ille Letiferi erroris, Gassendo nuper amatus Defensore novo speret se posse tueri.
“I fear that this branch of deadly error”—the atheism of Epicurus—“which Gassendi once loved, may hope to flourish again under this new defender”—Isaac Newton.
Th. Däubler, At the Sea — From Th. Däubler, Der sternhelle Weg, Leipzig 1919, p. 64.
The water demon dies … — From Theodor Däubler, Das Nordlicht, Geneva edition, Vol. 2, Leipzig 1922, Die Alexandrinische Phantasie (“Christmas Triptych”), p. 346.
Mythology of the dwarf — See Theodor Däubler, Das Nordlicht, Geneva edition, Vol. 2, Leipzig 1922, Der äthiopische Totentanz, pp. 160–168.
Whom you do not abandon, Genius! — Quotation from Goethe, “Wanderers Sturmlied.”
Konrad Weiß with his poem “1933” — This does not mean the opening poem titled “1933” from Der christliche Epimetheus; see p. 149.
Here Schmitt means the poem “Justitia,” written in 1933 and dedicated to Carl Schmitt.
deeply moved by the sentence from Ernst Jünger’s Strahlungen — Correctly:
“The good boy. From childhood onward, his aim was to follow his father’s example. Now, on his very first attempt, he has done it better and surpassed him beyond measure.”
See also Martin Tielke, Der stille Bürgerkrieg, Berlin 2007.
Gabba — Carlo Francesco Gabba (1835–1920), Italian jurist. See Nomos, p. 180.
whereas Hall — William Edward Hall (1835–1894), American scholar of international law.
